title: Towards Token-Level Text Anomaly Detection
summary: Existing text anomaly detection only flags whole documents, so the paper introduces token-level text anomaly detection and releases three annotated benchmarks (SMS spam character corruption, restaurant-review sentiment anomalies, grammar errors) with token-level labels. It proposes TokenCore, a PatchCore-style method that builds a memory bank of word-level BERT-base-uncased embeddings from normal training documents (element-wise max pooling over subwords), scores each test token by its nearest-neighbor distance in the bank, and averages token scores into a document score. Across the three datasets TokenCore attains the best average AUROC at both token level (0.7145) and document level (0.7335), ranking first on Review and Grammar at token level, while statistical baselines (ECOD, iForest) beat it on SMS_Spam.

match_target.why: The user hint targets Table 3, TokenCore token-level AUROC on Grammar; in the provided PDF text this value (0.6371) appears in Table 1's token-level block, Grammar ROC column (the PDF contains only Table 1, so the hint's 'Table 3' is presumably a different numbering of the same value). It is the cheapest claim that demonstrates the paper's central memory-bank localization result: no gradient training at all, just BERT-base embedding of 300 short sentences, a memory bank over the tokens of ~135 normal sentences, and brute-force nearest-neighbor scoring on CPU in minutes, on the paper's hardest dataset where every method stays below 0.65.

tolerance.why: Rule 3: AUROC is a bounded score (AUC-type) on a small evaluation set — the Grammar dataset has only 300 documents (30 anomalous), so the positives driving AUROC are the tokens of 30 short sentences, far below the 2,000-example threshold of rule 2; the paper reports no std or CI so rule 1 is inapplicable; and the paper prints AUROC as a fraction in [0,1], so the band is 0.02 absolute (equivalently 2.0 points), i.e., accept [0.6171, 0.6571] around 0.6371. The same 0.02 band is applied to the other fraction-scale AUROC/AUPRC claims on these small datasets.

requirements.stmt: Use bert-base-uncased as the shared embedding backbone for TokenCore and all baselines, with max pooling aggregation of subwords.
requirements.quote: All the methods operate on BERT-base-uncased embeddings with max pooling

requirements.stmt: Aggregate subword (WordPiece) embeddings into word-level token embeddings via element-wise max pooling (Eq. 1), not first-subword or average pooling.
requirements.quote: To maximize the anomaly signal for each token, we propose using max pooling to aggregate subword embeddings

requirements.stmt: Build the memory bank by encoding only normal training documents and storing their word-level token embeddings (no subsampling or coreset reduction is mentioned).
requirements.quote: Normal documents are encoded by LLM to construct a memory bank of normal token embeddings

requirements.stmt: Score each test token as its minimum distance to the memory bank (Eq. 2), with larger distance meaning more anomalous.
requirements.quote: A larger distance indicates higher anomaly score, as the token is farther from any normal token pattern in the embedding space.

requirements.stmt: Compute the document-level anomaly score as the mean of the token-level scores over all tokens of the document (Eq. 3).
requirements.quote: we aggregate token-level scores across all tokens in the document

requirements.stmt: Split each dataset so that 50% of normal documents form the training set (memory bank) and the remaining data, containing both normal and anomalous documents, is the test set.
requirements.quote: We use 50% normal documents as training data, the rest of data are set as testing including both normal and anomaly.

requirements.stmt: Report AUROC and AUPRC at both token and document levels, comparing TokenCore against the 6 baselines LOF, iForest, ECOD, Deep SVDD, AutoEncoder, and LUNAR (only the TokenCore rows are required for the match target).
requirements.quote: We compare TokenCore against 6 anomaly detection methods and use AUROC and AUPRC as evaluation metrics

requirements.stmt: Construct the Grammar evaluation set with 270 correct sentences as normal samples and 30 incorrect sentences as anomalous samples (10% anomaly rate).
requirements.quote: selecting 270 correct sentences as normal samples and 30 incorrect sentences as anomalous samples

requirements.stmt: Handle the fact that tokenizers split words into subwords: score at the word level (one embedding per word after subword aggregation) so results align with word-level token annotations.
requirements.cite: Section 5 Embedding Extraction with Max Pooling
requirements.quote: Since tokenizers often split words into multiple subword units

requirements.stmt: Follow the PatchCore memory-bank paradigm adapted to text: nearest-neighbor matching against stored normal embeddings rather than a trained density or reconstruction model.
requirements.quote: TokenCore adapts the memory bank paradigm from PatchCore [10] in computer vision to the text domain.

requirements.stmt: Use the official released code and data as the reference implementation and data source where available.
requirements.quote: All the codes and data are publicly available on https://github.com/charles-cao/TokenCore.

data.name: Grammar Correction Dataset (target dataset)
data.how_to_get: Download from the Kaggle link given in the paper's footnote 2: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/satishgunjal/grammar-correction?resource=download ; then select 270 correct sentences as normal and 30 incorrect sentences as anomalous per Section 4. The released TokenCore repo may also contain the authors' curated copy — prefer it if present.

data.name: SMS Spam dataset (character-corruption anomalies)
data.how_to_get: https://huggingface.co/datasets/kendx/NLP-ADBench/tree/main/datasets/sms_spam (paper footnote 1); anomalies are created by injecting gibberish character sequences such as 'jasdhnjsdb' into randomly selected portions of normal messages per Section 4, or use the authors' annotated version from the GitHub repo.

data.name: Restaurant Review dataset (semantic anomalies)
data.how_to_get: Collected by the authors from Google Maps reviews of a USA restaurant; no direct public URL in the paper — obtain it from https://github.com/charles-cao/TokenCore which states all data are released.

data.name: TokenCore official code and annotated data
data.how_to_get: https://github.com/charles-cao/TokenCore (stated in the abstract); use for the exact datasets, splits and token-level annotations if available.
